hints: Look carefully at what each photomicrograph shows. Can you see condensed chromosomes in all four cells, and has cytokinesis (splitting into two cells) happened in any of them yet?

Remember when DNA doubles in the cell cycle. A new daughter cell after cytokinesis is in G1 with unreplicated DNA, so which stages after S phase and before the cytoplasm divides will have twice that amount?
walkthrough:
**Define the baseline cell**

Think what a cell just after mitosis plus cytokinesis is like. It is a new daughter cell in early G1.

It has the normal chromosome number, but each chromosome is one chromatid with one DNA molecule. Call this 2C DNA.

**Work out when DNA is doubled**

During S phase of interphase, every DNA molecule is replicated. So from G2 onwards the cell has twice the DNA, 4C, until the cytoplasm divides.

That means prophase, metaphase, anaphase and telophase (before cytokinesis) all still contain 4C in the one cell.

**Identify cells 1 to 4**

Cell 1 shows chromosomes lined up in the middle, metaphase. Cell 3 shows long condensing chromosomes, prophase.

Cell 4 shows sister chromatids pulled apart, anaphase. Cell 2 shows two groups at opposite poles but still one cell, telophase before cytokinesis. All four are after S and before cytokinesis, so all have 4C, twice the G1 amount.

options.A: Correct. All of 1, 2, 3 and 4 are in mitosis after DNA replication and before cytokinesis, so each whole cell holds twice the DNA of a new G1 daughter cell.
options.B: Incorrect. Cell 3 (prophase) is also after S phase, so it also has doubled DNA and should be included.
options.C: Incorrect. Cells 2 and 4 in telophase and anaphase still have all the DNA in one cell, so they also have twice the G1 amount.
options.D: Incorrect. Cells 1 and 3 in metaphase and prophase have already replicated their DNA in S phase, so they also have twice the G1 amount.
